transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Well, I guess what brings me in is that I just cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. It's getting so frustrating. I'm a carpenter, and lately, just one saw starting up across the shop, or somebody walking past the office, will completely pull me off what I’m doing. 

Actually, speaking of the office, we have this new guy, Dave, and he wears these work boots that squeak so loudly on the concrete. I keep telling him he needs to condition the leather or something. My dad used to say you can tell everything you need to know about a man by how he takes care of his boots. He was a carpenter too, built half the houses in my hometown back in the day. We used to work together before he retired... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, my focus. Yeah, it's not just noises either. Even just a random thought about another job will pop into my head, and then I'm totally derailed. Before I know it, the whole day just gets away from me and I haven't finished the frame I was supposed to be working on. I actually meant to write down a list of things to tell you today, but I left the notepad on my kitchen counter right next to the toaster. Which reminds me, I really need to buy a new toaster, the coils on the left side are completely shot... but anyway, yeah, that's why I'm here.
Have you noticed any recent periods where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or needed much less sleep than usual, even though you didn't feel tired?

No, I can't say I've felt anything like that. I mean, my energy is just... normal, I guess? I definitely need my sleep. If I don't get my seven hours, I'm a wreck the next day. Especially with the kind of work I do, you know? Hauling lumber around at my age, you feel it in your joints. My knees have been giving me so much grief lately, actually. I think it's from all the kneeling when we were doing the flooring on that house over on Elm Street. Beautiful house, by the way. Wrap-around porch, original stained glass in the entryway... they don't make them like that anymore. The owner, Mrs. Higgins, she made us lemonade every single afternoon. Real lemons, too, not that powdered stuff. I tried making it her way once, but I put way too much sugar in it and my grandkids wouldn't even drink it. They're so picky these days, anyway... but no, no crazy energy or anything. Just regular tired.
Did you notice these kinds of concentration and distractibility problems back when you were a kid or young adult, or is this something that's really only started more recently?

Well, no, it's not new. It's actually been like this my whole life, I think. Even back in grade school—gosh, I must have been, I don't know, nine or ten? Way before I turned twelve, anyway. My teachers were always pulling my mother aside. They'd say, "She's a bright girl, but she's just so careless." I was always losing my homework, or I'd completely forget what the teacher just told us to do. I'd just sit there staring out the window at the playground instead of doing my seatwork. 

Speaking of playgrounds, they just tore down the old wooden one over at Centennial Park. It's a shame, really. I helped build that structure back in the late nineties. We used this beautiful, treated cedar. Smelled amazing when we were cutting it. Cedar has such a distinct smell, you know? It keeps the bugs away, too. My husband, bless his heart, he tried to build a cedar chest for our daughter's wedding, but he didn't measure the dovetail joints right, and the whole thing ended up completely crooked. We still have it sitting in the basement... holding old winter coats. I really need to take those coats to Goodwill. I heard they're doing a big coat drive this weekend at the Methodist church. 

But yeah, my mother used to get so frustrated with me about school. She'd say my head was in the clouds. So, definitely not a new thing.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes lifelong, pervasive difficulty sustaining attention with marked distractibility by external stimuli (noises, visual cues) and internal stimuli (tangential thoughts), leading to incomplete tasks (unfinished carpentry frames) and functional impairment at work. Onset was clearly before age 12 (grade school, ages 9-10), corroborated by teacher and parental reports of carelessness, lost homework, and inattentiveness during seatwork. Symptoms have persisted chronically into adulthood without periods of remission. Mood symptoms suggestive of mania/hypomania (elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, increased energy) were explicitly denied, ruling out bipolar disorder. There is no evidence of psychotic symptoms, thought disorder, or circumstantial speech due to a primary thought disorder - the tangentiality appears more consistent with distractibility and disorganized attention rather than formal thought disorder. The presentation is most consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation.
